facts: The House voted 211-204 to refer Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's impeachment articles to the House Judiciary Committee, a procedural move that effectively ends the impeachment effort before the current Congress session concludes.

Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) reintroduced the impeachment articles on Monday, accusing Hegseth of high crimes tied to U.S. military action against Iran and strikes on drug boats in the Caribbean and Eastern Pacific.
All Republicans except Massie voted to send the measure to committee; more than a dozen members missed the vote, including 11 Democrats, some of whom cited traffic issues for their absence.
During a briefing, Hegseth called the impeachment effort a 'farce' and 'sabotage.'
President Trump posted on Truth Social that the impeachment effort 'has miserably FAILED.'
House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries said after the vote, 'This is not the end of it. It's just the beginning.'
Separately, House Republicans elected Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) as the new minority leader, replacing Speaker Mike Johnson, who is stepping down after the midterm losses.
Per BBC, Democrats are set to take control of both chambers of Congress in January following midterm election gains, which could change the political calculus around future impeachment attempts.
ladder.analysis: The vote itself was not a judgment on Hegseth's guilt or innocence but a procedural maneuver: by referring Massie's impeachment articles to the GOP-led Judiciary Committee rather than allowing a direct floor vote, Republican leadership ensured the measure would stall with little time left in the current Congress. The outcome hinged largely on attendance — enough Democrats were absent that Republicans had a working majority in the chamber. Massie, the lone Republican to vote against tabling the measure, pressed the issue over Hegseth's role in military actions against Iran and drug-trafficking vessels. The episode also arrives amid broader shifts in House leadership, with Jim Jordan stepping into the minority leader role as Mike Johnson departs following midterm losses, setting up a House dynamic in which the Judiciary and Oversight committees are expected to play a role in future investigations into the Trump administration.

ladder.implications: With Democrats poised to gain control of both chambers in January, they could revisit the underlying questions raised by Massie's impeachment effort under different political leadership, making this procedural defeat likely a pause rather than a resolution.

stories.headline: Treasury Secretary Bessent moved to military base after Iranian threats

claims.text: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was relocated from his Georgetown, Washington D.C. home to a military base amid Iran-linked threats.
Security concerns about Bessent increased after the Wall Street Journal published a January 2025 article containing an aerial photo that allowed his Georgetown home's location to be geo-located.
A senior administration official told Fox News that threats against Bessent had reached 'more than an advanced stage.'
A Treasury Department spokesperson said Bessent 'will not be deterred' by the threats and 'remains committed' to the administration's economic pressure campaign against Iran.
In September, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said Iran has 'substantially increased' efforts to target Americans, including U.S. officials.

Other administration officials who have relocated to military or protected housing include White House chief of staff Stephen Miller, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth; former officials Pam Bondi and Tulsi Gabbard also lived on military bases.
Bessent has led 'Operation Economic Outcast,' a sanctions effort aimed at economically isolating Iran, which he has described as working toward the 'asphyxiation' of Iran's economy.

In February, the U.S. and Israel launched an air campaign against Iran; a preliminary June ceasefire collapsed after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the U.S. reinstated a blockade on Iranian ports.

stories.headline: Russia-Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi end with prisoner exchange deal but no major breakthrough
stories.byline: International & World desk · anchored on Reuters, AP
body: Two days of U.S.-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi concluded Wednesday with an agreement in principle on a large-scale prisoner of war exchange, but no breakthrough on ending the nearly five-year war sparked by Russia's full-scale invasion. The talks, the first between the delegations since February, were described by Ukrainian negotiator Davyd Arakhamia as 'one of the hardest,' adding that 'the Russians came with very strict directives, so it was extremely difficult to soften the discussion.' U.S. envoy Jared Kushner said the number of prisoners would be finalized on Thursday, and Russian state media reported the exchange could take place in two to three weeks. Alexander Zorin, a deputy chief of the Russian General Staff's information department, said it would be one of the biggest swaps after the 1,000 soldiers returned home last year.

The talks focused on post-war security architecture for Europe, with Kyiv seeking reassurances that allies would come to its aid if Ukraine is attacked again despite it not being a NATO member, and Moscow demanding limits on NATO's influence in Eastern Europe. Kushner said the U.S. hoped to 'create a new framework' of security between Ukraine, Russia and Europe that could 'secure lasting peace,' while Kremlin negotiator Vladimir Medinsky said the world needed a 'new' and 'fair' security system. Kushner acknowledged that territorial issues, particularly over Ukraine's Donetsk region, would be the hardest to settle, but said 'progress' was made on a post-war security framework. He added that 'there is no trust right now between the sides and that is to be expected after a conflict like this.'

Kushner and U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff are scheduled to travel to Moscow on Thursday to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin, then to Dublin to meet Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Kushner said one goal of the Moscow meeting is to try to get European countries added to the talks, which Moscow has opposed. European officials from Britain, NATO and various EU countries were in Abu Dhabi and met with U.S. and Ukrainian negotiators, but the Kremlin said its delegation had no contact with them. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said European representatives could eventually join peace talks but added their current statements 'don't indicate any desire on their part to contribute to movement along the path toward peace.'

Ukraine's peace negotiator Arakhamia said there was 'good momentum' from the talks toward reaching a solution before the end of the year and urged a second round to be organized as soon as possible. Medinsky said the meeting helped Moscow and Kyiv edge closer to peace, while Kremlin foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov described the talks as 'substantive and quite useful.' Zelenskyy, who did not attend, said on X that 'Ukraine's priority is to end the war as soon as possible with a dignified peace' and that 'Europe must be represented at every stage of real diplomacy.' Kushner cautioned that any agreement on a peacetime security framework is contingent on the war ending, but that cannot occur 'until there's an agreement on territory and on all other bilateral issues.'

stories.headline: Spain holds first general strike in 14 years over housing and wages ahead of elections
body: Spain experienced widespread disruption on Wednesday as the country held its first general strike in 14 years, called by the main unions over the high cost of living and a severe housing crisis. The strike, which affected transport, industry, and public services, comes less than three weeks before a snap parliamentary election on November 29, in which Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's Socialist Party is trailing in the polls. The two main unions, UGT and CCOO, reported "massive" and "very significant" participation, with stoppages of 90% in the automotive and port sectors, 85% in the meat industry, 82% in waste collection, and 75% in the energy sector. However, the Spanish Confederation of Business Organizations described participation as "low and uneven."

The strike was triggered by widespread anger over unaffordable housing, which was galvanized by the eviction in September of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from a Madrid flat where she had lived for seven decades after her rent was tripled; she died in hospital weeks later. Rental prices have soared across Spain, with the average monthly cost of a 50-square-meter apartment in Madrid reaching €1,170 in October, according to property portal Idealista, while the average gross monthly salary is about €2,460 — meaning rent consumes nearly half of gross pay, far above the recommended 30% threshold. The Bank of Spain estimates that 750,000 new homes are needed to meet current demand, yet only 92,000 were built in 2025. The country's youth council says a young person would need to spend 98.7% of their monthly salary to rent alone, and many, like 35-year-old Arturo, say they cannot afford to move out of their parents' homes.

Disruption was heaviest in the main industrial hubs of Madrid and the northeastern region of Catalonia, where traffic was halted on several major roads. In Barcelona, public transport faced long delays or was at a standstill during the morning rush hour, while in Madrid, city buses were hardest hit. Minor incidents were reported, including roadblocks with burning tires in Barcelona and scuffles between picketers and police near Madrid's main wholesale market. The interior ministry said dozens of people were arrested for various incidents, and Spanish media reported attacks on estate agency offices. Power usage in Spain fell by 7.5% during the early hours of the strike, according to data from operator Red Eléctrica, compared with a drop of more than 15% during the last general strike 14 years ago.

The strike has drawn an unusual political response. Prime Minister Sánchez, who called the snap election after parliament failed to approve his housing reform plan, has encouraged workers to participate, writing on social media that previous strikes secured "collective conquests" such as the eight-hour day, pensions, and public healthcare. In contrast, the conservative People's Party (PP), which leads in the polls, accused the government of exploiting the strike for electoral gain. PP leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo called the strike "nonsense" and referred to the unions as "mafia" and "trash," while party spokesman Miguel Tellado said the government was using the strike to warn voters against allowing a right-wing government to form. Sánchez responded that it is "nonsense to question the rights of workers to strike."

The unions are demanding more government intervention in the housing market, including the elimination of tourist apartments, a crackdown on real estate speculation, automatic renewal of leases for renters, and a new minimum wage agreement through talks with business owners. The vice-president of Spain's largest business association, CEOE, criticized the strike as political rather than labor-related, saying businesses have little to do with housing prices. Demonstrations were planned in major cities, and the scale of support is widely seen as an indicator of public discontent ahead of the election. Among those striking was 27-year-old Gonzalo Álvarez, who knew Maricarmen and volunteers for a housing union; he pays €1,000 in rent with his girlfriend for a one-bedroom flat in Madrid, with each spending about half their salary on housing. "It's absolutely crazy," he said. "With the food, with the electricity, with the water, with gas."

stories.headline: British counterterrorism police arrest US soldier accused of spying for Russia
body: British counterterrorism police have arrested a 41-year-old member of the US Army near Gloucester, England, on suspicion of espionage activity in connection with Russia. The Metropolitan Police confirmed the arrest on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, and said authorities searched two locations in the Gloucestershire region. The man was taken into custody at a London police station, with investigators from the US and UK involved in the probe.

Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans, Senior National Coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing, called it a "significant arrest" resulting from "close collaboration between UK and US authorities." She added: "The allegations are serious and our investigation is very much ongoing." FBI Director Kash Patel said the case was of "utmost concern" to the US and its allies, and declared: "This FBI has no tolerance for anyone who breaks their oath to the United States and whose actions endanger our national security and that of our partners." Patel thanked UK investigators and the US Military Counterintelligence Command for their work.

Brigadier General Sean Stinchon, commanding general of US Army Counterintelligence Command, said the case demonstrated the "resolve of the counterintelligence community." He described the alleged conduct of a senior soldier entrusted with sensitive information as "a sobering reminder that insider threats are real and persistent."

The Gloucestershire area, about two hours' drive from London, hosts several sensitive military and intelligence sites, including RAF Fairford, a large airbase used by both UK and US planes, and the nearby town of Cheltenham, home to the headquarters of Britain's signals intelligence agency GCHQ. The Metropolitan Police noted that US authorities, the US Military, and the FBI were closely involved in the investigation, which remains ongoing.

stories.headline: COP31 in Turkey: Guterres calls for climate justice tax, Thunberg blasts 'hypocrisy', US absent
stories.byline: International & World desk · anchored on Reuters
body: World leaders gathered in Antalya, Turkey, on Wednesday for the COP31 climate summit, where UN Secretary-General António Guterres warned that the planet is heading toward more than 2.5°C of warming by century's end and proposed a 'climate justice compact' that includes taxing fossil fuel companies. 'Our planet is heating up. The clock is winding down. It's make or bake time,' Guterres said, urging governments to tax windfall profits from oil giants. He contrasted the $95 billion earned by the world's nine largest oil companies in one quarter with the roughly $600 million received by the international fund for climate-related loss and damage—equivalent to just 14 hours of those companies' profits. 'Polluters must pay,' he declared, earning an ovation. The United States is not attending the summit, which runs until Nov. 20.

Climate activist Greta Thunberg, attending her first COP since 2021, condemned the talks as 'hypocrisy' and accused host countries of using the forum to 'whitewash themselves.' 'Our political and economic systems that have become incompatible with human nature,' she said, warning that 'everything and everyone we love is at stake.' Her arrival energized youth activists, including Amber Turner of the Alliance of Small Island States, who said Thunberg's presence 'reminds us of why we started this work in the first place.' Protests at the conference demanded more climate finance and criticized growing interest in nuclear energy.

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, co-host with Australia, acknowledged that three decades of climate negotiations had failed to deliver sufficient results. 'This success at the level of ideas has not produced the same results when it comes to implementation,' he said. Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva warned that wars and trade disputes are overshadowing climate action: 'We started talking more about weapons and tariffs than the survival of future generations.' Turkey is promoting global electrification, aiming for electricity to account for 35% of global energy consumption by 2035, up from 23% today, though both co-hosts still rely heavily on fossil fuels, especially coal.

Methane featured prominently during Wednesday's 'Zero Waste' thematic day. Guterres called on the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) to develop a global standard for near-zero methane emissions from oil and gas. UNEP's Julia Ferini described methane as 'our climate emergency brake,' noting that cutting this short-lived gas could slow warming relatively quickly. UNEP has tracked major leaks from space, issuing more than 5,000 alerts since 2023, but barely one in eight has received a response. The summit also highlighted youth-led solutions, such as a Botswana company using worms to compost organic waste, processing over 1,000 tonnes. COP32 is scheduled for Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, in November 2027.

stories.headline: Indonesia's vice president offers resignation amid court ruling and political rift
body: Indonesia's Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka has offered his resignation to President Prabowo Subianto, an aide confirmed, as a Supreme Court ruling questioning his educational credentials and growing tensions between Prabowo and former President Joko Widodo threaten the ruling alliance. Gibran's aide Budi Arie told the BBC that the resignation letter was submitted directly to Prabowo on Wednesday; it remains unclear whether the president has accepted it. State Secretariat Minister Prasetyo Hadi said the two held over two hours of talks on Tuesday, and that Prabowo advised Gibran to 'continue pursuing legal avenues to defend the validity of his academic documents.'

The resignation offer follows an Indonesian Supreme Court ruling that a high-school document used during Gibran's 2024 election campaign was invalid. The court found 'no evidence was found to show Gibran had a foreign diploma or certificate that could serve as the basis for equivalency with a senior high school or equivalent qualification.' Gibran, who studied in Singapore and Australia, had used an Indonesian equivalence certificate to meet legal requirements. The ruling prompted more than 100 lawmakers to support a parliamentary initiative that could have led to impeachment proceedings. Gibran previously argued that undertaking university education was sufficient proof of completing senior high school; on Tuesday he asked for a chance to challenge the ruling.

Gibran's resignation comes amid signs that the political alliance between Prabowo and former President Joko Widodo (Jokowi) is fraying. Gibran, Jokowi's son, was added to Prabowo's 2024 ticket after a controversial Constitutional Court ruling exempted him from the minimum age requirement of 40. Since taking office, Prabowo has shifted focus away from Jokowi's legacy project of building a new capital, Nusantara, toward his own free school meals programme. He has also reshuffled personnel, moving Jokowi loyalists including long-serving finance minister Sri Mulyani Indrawati into new roles. Last week, authorities arrested presidential chief of staff Listyo Sigit Prabowo on suspicions of wiretapping the president; Prabowo sacked him a day later. Listyo, a former national police chief, is widely considered a longtime Jokowi ally.

Within the government, allegiances appear to be shifting. On Monday, three members of Prabowo's cabinet collectively resigned from the party led by Kaesang Pangarep, Jokowi's youngest son, citing a desire to focus on their duties in Prabowo's administration. Separately, Jokowi faces unrelated allegations that he used a fake university diploma, which he denies.

The political turmoil unfolds at a turbulent period for Prabowo's presidency. The free school meals programme is struggling for funding, parts of Indonesia have battled the country's worst wildfires in a decade, and the national stock market faces crisis amid allegations of widespread market manipulation. On Tuesday, students across the country staged demonstrations to protest the government's handling of environmental issues and corruption. In a brief statement, Gibran said: 'I respect all criticism and feedback from the public regarding the developments that are taking place. I do not want the current situation to become a prolonged political controversy.'

stories.headline: Anthropic IPO demand surges as Nvidia faces scrutiny; Microsoft stake raises questions
body: Anthropic, the U.S.-based artificial intelligence company behind the Claude model, said in an updated filing Tuesday that it will offer 825 million shares in its upcoming initial public offering at a price range between $70 and $78 per share. Trading on the Nasdaq is expected to begin on Nov. 19, according to people familiar with the details. The IPO is reportedly seeing very strong demand, with big money already lining up during the roadshow, despite broader concerns over the AI trade.

Microsoft, a strategic investor in Anthropic, is taking a roughly $1 billion stake in the concurrent placement, representing about 13,513,513 shares at the $74 midpoint. The stake equals approximately 0.03% of Microsoft's $3.97 trillion market value. The filing discloses that Anthropic sells Claude through AWS, Google Cloud and Microsoft Azure under joint go-to-market arrangements in which it pays each cloud provider a fee. Anthropic also reports about $900.9 billion of aggregate committed spend on purchase commitments and leases, mostly for compute and infrastructure, without a counterparty breakdown. Fortune reported the offering could value Anthropic at up to $1.4 trillion on a fully diluted basis. Microsoft shares declined 2.5% to $532.44 in regular trading Wednesday, trading 11.5% below GuruFocus's GF Value of $601.35, which the firm calls 'Modestly Undervalued.'

Meanwhile, Nvidia faces mounting scrutiny. A Baird analyst downgraded the stock, warning of major scrutiny ahead and no longer recommending buying the chip maker's shares. News of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy involved with an entity that short seller Culper Research alleged helped Alibaba obtain restricted Nvidia chips has dragged down the stock to its lowest valuation since late March, weighing on the overall U.S. stock market. Despite the downgrade, Nvidia shares rose nearly 4% in pre-market trading Wednesday. Goldman Sachs said the company's third-quarter results are expected to exceed expectations. A Seeking Alpha analyst rated Nvidia a Hold at $169, with a fair value estimate of $145, citing risks including unsustainable 75% gross margins, customer financing exposure, and aggressive revenue guidance.

In China, Alibaba announced late Tuesday that the Hong Kong Stock Exchange will allow it to spin off its semiconductor subsidiary T-Head via a public offering in Hong Kong, subject to approval from the exchange and the China Securities Regulatory Commission. The filing did not disclose a date or proposed size. Alibaba noted it had already filed confidentially on Sept. 11. Hong Kong-listed shares of Alibaba traded 1% lower Wednesday and are down about 29% year-to-date. In late September, Alibaba announced its next-generation AI chip, the Zhenwu V900, which it said delivers three times the performance of its predecessor. Alibaba is one of several Chinese companies developing homegrown semiconductors amid growing U.S. restrictions on China's access to chips. Short seller Culper Research alleged in May that Alibaba was able to obtain restricted Nvidia chips by indirectly financing entities in Southeast Asia; Alibaba did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Other Chinese tech IPOs face delays. Baidu has reportedly delayed the listing of its AI chip entity Kunlunxin, and Chinese memory chip company YMTC has also delayed its listing, according to news reports this month. Neither company immediately responded to requests for comment. In recent months, China's financial regulators have increased their scrutiny on tech IPOs and the rush of capital into the sector. Chinese tech stocks have underperformed their U.S. peers, despite investor excitement last year around AI breakthroughs by DeepSeek.

The developments highlight a volatile period for AI-related stocks, with Anthropic's IPO drawing strong demand even as Nvidia faces reputational and competitive pressures. Microsoft's $1 billion stake in Anthropic tests the balance between partner and rival, as Claude routes revenue through Azure while potentially competing with Microsoft's own software. Investors will watch for any Azure-specific disclosure of Anthropic spending and monitor Nvidia's upcoming earnings for signs of sustained growth.

stories.headline: October CPI rises 0.4%, more than expected, fueling rate-hike fears
body: Consumer prices rose more than expected in October, a fresh warning sign for the Federal Reserve as it weighs its next interest-rate move. The consumer price index increased a seasonally adjusted 0.4% for the month, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Tuesday, above the 0.3% gain economists surveyed by Dow Jones had forecast. Excluding volatile food and energy, core CPI rose 0.3%, also topping expectations for a 0.2% increase. The headline CPI had risen 0.6% in September, while core was up 0.3%.

The report comes at a critical juncture for the Fed. Speaking Tuesday morning before the release, Fed Governor Christopher Waller said a hot inflation report could push him toward advocating for a half-point increase in December, specifically noting such a hike should be on the table if core CPI came in 'around 0.3.' Hours later, that is exactly what happened. Traders are now fully pricing in a quarter-point increase at the Fed's Dec. 8-9 meeting, with odds of a half-point hike at 13.6%, up from near zero before the report, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool. Stocks fell following the release, with the Nasdaq composite dropping 0.7% and the S&P 500 falling 0.4%, while Treasury yields jumped.

Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan, speaking after the report, said she sees a need for two additional quarter-point increases, noting the CPI reading was 'higher than expected' and expressing worry that the Fed's primary inflation-forecasting metric, the personal consumption expenditures price index, could also move higher. 'It may be possible to move more rapidly this winter than the [Federal Open Market Committee] has moved so far this fall,' she said. Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson said the data suggests 'inflation pressures are still very much with us' and that 'further gradual tightening seems appropriate.' At its October meeting, the Fed voted 10-2 to keep its benchmark rate in a range between 3.75% and 4% while awaiting incoming data.

The BLS did not estimate a yearly rate in its October report; the government shutdown last year prevented the bureau from collecting sufficient data in October 2025, leaving no comparable figure. However, the report included annual figures for some individual items. The energy index rose 0.7%, with gasoline up 1%, though natural gas fell 0.8%. Food costs accelerated 0.5%, pushed higher by increases of 1% for snacks, 0.9% for beef, and 0.5% for meats, poultry, fish, and eggs. Shelter costs rose 0.3%, accounting for more than 30% of the headline increase. Transportation services jumped 0.8%, while new vehicle prices increased 0.2% and used cars and trucks fell 1.2%. Apparel rose just 0.1%, and medical care commodities increased 0.5%. Electricity prices rose 0.9%, a potential complication from the artificial intelligence buildout, which has been pressuring inflation alongside tariffs and the Iran war.

Despite moderating gas prices recently, Fed officials have expressed concern that the impacts from the Iran war and President Donald Trump's tariffs are becoming embedded in the economy. Inflation has been running above the Fed's 2% target for some 5½ years. A net 37% of businesses responding to the October National Federation of Independent Business survey reported plans to raise prices in the next three months, the highest level since July 2022. 'This was the report the market could least afford to see,' said Karen Manna, fixed income investment strategist at Federated Hermes. 'A hotter inflation print raises fresh questions about whether the Fed has done enough to contain price pressures and reinforces the risk that interest rates need to move higher and stay there for longer.'

stories.headline: Pochettino ready to accept Man Utd offer to replace Carrick
body: Mauricio Pochettino is ready to accept an offer from Manchester United to become their next head coach, with the club having opened talks with the Argentine about replacing Michael Carrick, who is expected to be relieved of his duties in the next 48 hours. Sources have told BBC Sport that USA manager Pochettino wants to take the job once Carrick's future is clarified. US Soccer officials are expecting an official approach from United and have a contingency plan for their manager's departure, including a succession plan. United would be required to pay $10m (£7.5m) to release Pochettino from his contract, which he signed in August.

Carrick's future at United will be decided at a meeting in Monaco on Wednesday attended by chief executive Omar Berrada, director of football Jason Wilcox and co-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe. Berrada and Wilcox have flown to Monaco for one of their regular, planned meetings to discuss strategy, with the main issue being Carrick's future and what should happen next. It is expected that Berrada and Wilcox's recommendation is for the head coach to go. Carrick, 45, was pictured arriving at the club's Carrington training base on Wednesday. United are 18th in the Premier League, inside the relegation zone, after winning just one of their first 10 games and none since August. It is the club's lowest position at this stage of a top-flight season since 1986-87, when they were 20th.

Pochettino, 54, is understood to view the prospect of managing United as a serious opportunity, with the expectation he would accept the job were it formally offered. United have spoken to the former Argentina defender about their managerial position on three previous occasions: when Jose Mourinho was sacked in 2018, in 2022 before the club appointed Erik ten Hag, and again when Ten Hag was sacked in 2024. Pochettino's first Premier League job was at Southampton from January 2013, followed by a five-year stint at Tottenham from 2014 that included a Champions League final appearance. He managed Paris St-Germain from January 2021 to July 2022 before spending the 2023-24 season in charge of Chelsea. He moved into international football by taking the USA job in September 2024 and led the co-hosts to the last 16 of the 2026 World Cup.

The USA have a two-legged Concacaf Nations League quarter-final against Haiti over the next week. With confidence over a succession plan, it raises the possibility that Pochettino may not take charge of those games. On Thursday, US Soccer cancelled planned media with players, citing a clash with Veterans Day, though some reports claimed it was to stop the squad being asked about their manager. Pochettino wants to remain respectful to the US Soccer Federation and will wait for United to make their approach.

Pochettino and United go back a long way, with his name associated with the club since he was spotted leaving a lunch appointment with Sir Alex Ferguson in 2016. Ferguson was three years into his retirement, while Pochettino was building his reputation at Tottenham. Pochettino called it 'a meeting in London between colleagues, between a genius and an apprentice.' He was mentioned as a contender to succeed Louis van Gaal when he was sacked by United in May 2016, then when Mourinho suffered the same fate in December 2018. Pochettino was the other name on United's shortlist when Ten Hag was appointed in April 2022, then again when the Dutchman was shown the door in October 2024.

While it may seem a touch immoral for Manchester United to be talking to a potential new manager before they have decided if their current one is staying or not, this kind of situation is not uncommon in football. Jose Mourinho had agreed a contract with United in 2016 before Louis van Gaal was sacked, which is how stories came out that the Dutchman would be dismissed as he was celebrating the FA Cup final triumph over Crystal Palace. stories.headline: Vikings trade for Kirk Cousins after Raiders gave QB option to stay or leave
body: The Minnesota Vikings acquired quarterback Kirk Cousins from the Las Vegas Raiders at Tuesday's 4 p.m. ET trade deadline, sending a 2027 third-round pick to reunite with their former starter. Before the deal was finalized, the Raiders gave Cousins the choice of whether to leave the organization or remain with the club he had started the first nine games of the 2026 season for, according to The Ringer's Tom Pelissero. After consulting with his family, agent Mike McCartney, and Vikings head coach Kevin O'Connell, Cousins decided by midday Tuesday to return to Minnesota and informed Raiders general manager John Spytek of his decision.

"So much respect for John Spytek and the Raiders organization," McCartney told Pelissero. "There aren't many leaders in this league who would've done that. Very appreciative of Spy." Part of Cousins' calculus was the presence of rookie Fernando Mendoza, the No. 1 overall pick in the 2026 draft. The report indicated Cousins knew it was only a matter of time before the Raiders turned the franchise over to Mendoza, making his status as QB1 fleeting. With an opportunity to help a Vikings team he spent six years with and won the NFC North in 2022, the pieces fell into place for the deal.

Cousins, 38, has the most single-season passing touchdowns (20) and career passing touchdowns (318) by any quarterback changing teams midseason in NFL history. During his first six-year stint with the Vikings, he ranked second in completion percentage (67.9%), fourth in passing yards (23,265), and third in passing touchdowns (171) among all quarterbacks with at least 50 starts. He reunites with wide receiver Justin Jefferson, who averaged 98.9 receiving yards per game with Cousins — an NFL record for most receiving yards by a quarterback-receiver duo over at least 50 games. The Vikings' offense is tied for the fewest offensive touchdowns (11) in the NFL this season.

FOX Sports' Henry McKenna graded the trade an A for the Raiders and a C+ for the Vikings, noting that Las Vegas gets a Day 2 draft pick while moving on to Mendoza. McKenna expressed skepticism about Minnesota's move, citing the team's recent instability at quarterback — including moving to J.J. McCarthy last year and then moving on from him, and Carson Wentz's poor performance filling in for an injured Kyler Murray. Cousins is on a $10 million deal for this year, but McKenna called the third-round pick a high price given that the Murray signing was supposed to provide value. "In Minnesota, there's a plan. Then there's a new plan. Then there's a new plan again," McKenna wrote. "Forgive me for not fully buying this one."

stories.headline: Rex Ryan arrested on 6 charges after striking pedestrians with truck
body: Former NFL head coach and current ESPN broadcaster Rex Ryan surrendered to Nashville police Wednesday morning and faces six charges after allegedly striking two pedestrians with his pickup truck on Nov. 5. The incident occurred shortly before midnight as the pedestrians were crossing Broadway from 4th Avenue with a walk signal, according to Metro Nashville Police. Both victims suffered minor injuries; Ryan's truck ran over their feet and made contact with one individual's leg.

Police said the pedestrians had the right of way. After striking them, the vehicle continued driving but stopped at a red light at Broadway and Representative John Lewis Way. The pedestrians approached the truck and confronted the driver. According to police, 'The pedestrians said the vehicle kept going, but stopped for the red light at Broadway and Representative John Lewis Way where they waved down the driver. They said he stepped out of the truck to argue with them, got back in, and drove away.' The pedestrians took pictures of the driver and the truck's license plate, which was registered to Ryan.

Ryan, 63, was charged with two counts of leaving the scene of an accident, two counts of failure to give information or render aid, and two counts of failure to obey a traffic control signal. His bond was set at $6,000 by a judicial commissioner. He is scheduled to appear in a Nashville courtroom on December 18.

Ryan began his NFL coaching career with the Arizona Cardinals in 1994 as a defensive line and linebackers coach. He later joined the Baltimore Ravens in 1999 as a defensive line coach, helping the team win Super Bowl XXXV, and became defensive coordinator in 2005. He became head coach of the New York Jets in 2008, leading them to consecutive AFC Championship Game appearances. After being dismissed by the Jets in December 2014, he coached the Buffalo Bills until his tenure ended in December 2016. Ryan's head coaching record is 65-68 (4-2 in the playoffs). He has since worked as an NFL analyst for ESPN.

stories.headline: Astros hire Brad Ausmus as manager, bringing franchise icon back to Houston
body: The Houston Astros have named Brad Ausmus as their next manager, the team announced Wednesday. Ausmus, 57, replaces Joe Espada, whose contract was not renewed after three seasons in which he led the Astros to the playoffs twice. The hiring is the first major move by general manager Randy Flores, who was named to his post earlier in the offseason.

Ausmus, a former Astros catcher who spent 10 of his 18 major-league seasons in Houston, had served as bench coach for the New York Yankees since late 2023. He previously managed the Detroit Tigers from 2014 to 2017, compiling a 314-332 record and winning the American League Central in his first season, and the Los Angeles Angels in 2019, going 72-90. His career managerial winning percentage is .478.

"I am very excited to be back in Houston," Ausmus said in a statement. "The Astros and the city of Houston have been a huge part of my life, and I'm thrilled to create a new chapter as the team's manager. I'd like to thank [general manager Randy Flores] and the entire Astros organization for this opportunity, and I can't wait to get to work." Flores added: "Brad impressed us throughout the interview process, demonstrating the leadership, energy, and expertise critical to driving a winning culture both on and off the field."

The Astros are coming off a 2026 season in which they won the American League West with an 81-81 record and a negative run differential, then were swept out of the Wild Card round by the Chicago White Sox. The team has made the ALCS in seven straight seasons from 2017 to 2023, winning two World Series titles, but has not returned since. The roster features several core players—including Yordan Alvarez, Jeremy Peña, Isaac Paredes, Hunter Brown, Christian Walker, Yainer Diaz, Cristian Javier, and Josh Hader—who are slated for free agency after 2027 or 2028, and the farm system is considered weak after years of contention and draft penalties related to the sign-stealing scandal.

Ausmus becomes the first manager hired under Flores, who replaced Dana Brown earlier in the offseason. The hiring also reunites Ausmus with former teammate Jeff Bagwell, a key advisor to owner Jim Crane. Ausmus was connected to previous Astros managerial openings and even to the general manager position over the years. With the move, the Los Angeles Angels are now the only team with a managerial vacancy. The Yankees will need to find a new bench coach.

stories.headline: U.S. on verge of losing measles elimination status as cases surge
stories.byline: Health & Science desk · anchored on Reuters
body: The United States is almost certain to lose its measles elimination status this week as a committee of the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) meets to assess the disease's spread in the Americas. The PAHO Measles and Rubella Elimination Regional Monitoring and Re-Verification Commission began a four-day meeting on November 10, during which an international panel of experts will decide whether the U.S. has maintained elimination, which it was declared to have achieved in 2000. All signs point to a negative ruling, public health experts say, as measles cases have soared in recent years and at least eight deaths have been reported in 2026.

So far in 2026, the U.S. has recorded 5,182 confirmed measles cases, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, up from 2,289 in all of 2025 and just 285 in 2024. The disease has been detected in nearly every state, and local health departments have reported eight deaths connected to the outbreaks this year; the CDC has recorded four deaths. More than 40 percent of cases this year have occurred in people aged 20 or older, and 96 percent of all cases were in individuals who were either unvaccinated or whose vaccination status was unknown. The percentage of kindergartners who received the MMR vaccine has fallen to 92.4 percent in 2026, down from 95.2 percent in 2020, below the 95 percent threshold needed for herd immunity. Eighteen states have MMR vaccination rates below 90 percent, with Idaho reporting a rate of just 75.2 percent. A study in Nature Health in January found numerous counties across the country with MMR coverage under 60 percent.

Losing elimination status would hold no formal consequences but would represent a significant public health failure for the wealthiest country in the world, experts said. Michael Osterholm, director of the Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy at the University of Minnesota, said revoking the status would merely recognize what has been a fact on the ground for months. "When a semi hits your car at 60 miles an hour at an intersection, you don't need more assessments showing you've had an accident," he said. Elizabeth Jacobs, a professor emeritus at the University of Arizona and member of the Coordinating Committee of Defend Public Health, expressed dismay: "It's astounding to me. I'm just beside myself about all of this. I literally cannot believe this is happening in the United States."

Many public health experts blame the Department of Health and Human Services under Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a longtime vaccine critic. Jacobs described the department as an "epidemiological crime scene." While Kennedy has occasionally recommended that parents get their children the MMR vaccine, he has also recommended ineffective treatments for measles and has sown doubt about vaccine safety for years. "He has had ample time to go and form a really rigorous and thorough vaccination program, and he can barely say that MMR vaccination is the only way to prevent measles effectively," Jacobs said. HHS did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In January, then-CDC official Ralph Abraham told STAT that losing elimination status would be "the cost of doing business."

Osterholm warned that the situation could worsen, pointing to Canada, which lost its measles elimination status last year after recording more than 5,000 cases in a population of 40 million. The U.S. population is roughly 350 million. Vaccination rates vary widely within states, creating pockets of unprotected individuals. "There's an old line that describes this well: When your head's in the freezer and your feet are in the oven, you're, on average, very comfortable," Osterholm said. He noted that in Minnesota, a state with a progressive public health department, some schools have 80 percent vaccination levels while others are at 40 percent. The PAHO committee is expected to announce its decision by the end of the meeting on November 13.

stories.headline: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with alleged Chinese spy triggers board investigation, stock slide
stories.byline: Tech / AI desk · anchored on Reuters
body: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has admitted to an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, an executive at Nvidia customer Megaspeed whom U.S. intelligence agencies believe was spying for China, plunging the world's second-most-valuable company into a governance crisis. Nvidia's board announced Sunday it would conduct an independent investigation led by outside counsel Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz. The stock fell 5.47% on Tuesday and 4% on Monday, a two-day loss of about 9.5%, as investors absorbed the scandal and the prospect that Huang, who co-founded the chipmaker more than 30 years ago, could be forced out.

The board said in a Sunday statement that Nvidia 'has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised.' However, U.S. officials allege Alice Huang was a Chinese spy, and the affair has drawn scrutiny from Washington policymakers pressuring Huang to appear before congressional committees. Huang hired a PR crisis firm known for handling sex scandals a full year ago, according to Wired, though it is unclear when he learned of the espionage allegations. Corporate governance experts say there is no precedent for a CEO caught in a suspected honeypot, with the investigation's outcome depending heavily on what Huang knew and when.

Nvidia's chips are central to the AI boom, powering tools like ChatGPT, and Huang has personally backed hundreds of billions of dollars in investments and guarantees for AI startups and data center providers. Analysts at Bernstein wrote, 'Nvidia is not an ordinary company and Jensen is not an ordinary CEO; he IS Nvidia.' Sequoia Capital partner Shaun Maguire posted, 'Jensen is irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership.' Yet the company has no obvious successor, with a famously flat structure of more than 60 direct reports to Huang. His children also work at Nvidia: son Spencer as a director of product management, daughter Madison as a senior director of product marketing, and son-in-law Nico Caprez in business development. Huang did not rule out Madison as a potential successor when asked by Bloomberg last month.

The scandal has also highlighted broader concerns about Chinese economic espionage in the semiconductor industry. Nate Singer, CEO of due diligence firm Heron Intelligence, told TechCrunch that similar cases involving senior executives and state-sponsored actors are 'an open secret' in the industry, with many going unreported. 'There are a lot of senior people in the industry that know this is happening, and are effectively condoning it,' Singer said. He described a case where a CEO's wife confronted executives over a corporate jet used to fly with 'young ladies who also turned out to be state-sponsored actors.'

Nvidia already faces a proposed class action lawsuit alleging that Huang and the company misled investors by concealing the relationship while describing dealings with Alice Huang's former employer as routine. University of Colorado corporate governance professor Ann Lipton said securities fraud claims are 'only about lying,' adding, 'You can have as many affairs with Chinese spies as you like — you just can’t lie about it under the federal securities laws.' A mismanagement claim under Delaware law would be harder, requiring proof that the board cannot handle the problem independently. Huang owns about 3.6% of Nvidia and does not have dual-class voting control, making him 'easier to dislodge,' Lipton said.

stories.headline: Anthropic Founders to Cash Out $250M Each in IPO; CEO Predicts Cancer Cure in 10 Years
body: Anthropic, the artificial intelligence company founded by former OpenAI employees, has disclosed in its S-1 filing that each of its seven co-founders plans to sell approximately 3.38 million shares in its upcoming initial public offering. At the midrange of the company's unusually broad initial price range of $70 to $78 per share, each founder would net just shy of $250 million. At the low end, each would pocket just over $236 million; at the high end, just under $264 million. The IPO could value Anthropic at up to $1.4 trillion, with bankers reportedly suggesting the valuation could rise to $1.5 trillion due to excess demand.

The seven co-founders are CEO Dario Amodei; President and Chair of the Board Daniela Amodei; Chief Compute Officer Tom Brown; Head of Public Benefit Jack Clark; Chief Science Officer Jared Kaplan; Chief Architect Sam McCandlish; and Interpretability Research Lead Christopher Olah. After the sale, each will own about 3.2% of the outstanding Class A shares, or roughly 22% collectively. However, other holders, including Amazon and Google, hold nonvoting Class N shares, so the founders' stake in total equity will be considerably smaller. Each founder will also receive one share of Class F stock with supervoting rights, giving the group 51.1% of the votes, with no single founder holding significantly more shares or votes than the others.

The S-1 filing hints at strong demand: board member Reed Hastings has indicated he wants to buy $300 million worth of shares through his donor-advised fund, and board member Christopher Liddell wants to buy $3 million worth. The seven founders left OpenAI in 2021 after disagreements over how AI should be built, forming Anthropic with a stated focus on AI safety. Siblings Dario and Daniela Amodei had held senior research and policy roles at OpenAI, joined by five fellow OpenAI colleagues.

The company has recently released new models, Mythos and Fable 5.2, with Fable built with strong cybersecurity and biology safeguards against misuse, following extensive prerelease safety testing. Anthropic has hired David LaBianca, formerly a managing director and chief cybersecurity architect at Goldman Sachs and later a senior director of security engineering at Google, as a member of technical staff working on security engineering. The hire aligns with Anthropic's historic focus on AI safety.

Meanwhile, the traffic between finance and AI is not entirely one-way: Nataniel Ruiz, a PhD computer scientist and DeepMind researcher focused on generative photo and video models, has left Google to join Citadel's equity quantitative research team. Anthropic, Google, and Citadel declined to comment on the moves. Anthropic's IPO filing marks a significant milestone for the company, which was valued closer to $18 billion in 2024, and employees who joined earlier may now see substantial payouts.

stories.headline: Google DeepMind uses AI to formally verify Signal's encryption protocol
body: Google DeepMind researchers have used a new AI framework called AlphaProof Code to mathematically prove, or formally verify, key security guarantees in the compiled code of the Signal protocol, the encryption technology that protects billions of conversations in apps like Signal, Google Messages, and WhatsApp. The four-week proof-of-concept project, announced on November 10, marks the first time AI has been used to formally verify a widely deployed cryptographic protocol at this depth, and the first time the implementation of such a protocol has been formally verified by any method.

The analysis focused on two core components of the Signal protocol: PQXDH, the handshake that establishes a shared secret at the start of a conversation, and the Triple Ratchet, which updates the keys used to encrypt messages. The researchers proved properties including forward secrecy, which keeps earlier messages protected if an attacker later steals current session keys, and that protection for future messages can recover after fresh key material is exchanged. They also separately proved handshake secrecy in a model simulating a future quantum threat. The verification covered an executable built for 64-bit Arm processors from version 0.105.4 of libsignal, the protocol's reference implementation.

Formal verification uses mathematics to check that software functions as intended without critical vulnerabilities, but it has traditionally been extremely time-consuming, requiring experts to describe software properties, convert them into formulas, and develop proofs. AlphaProof Code, a multi-LLM agentic framework, splits the work: human experts collaborated with AI to translate Signal's security goals into formal mathematical specifications, then agents powered by Gemini Carbon generated over six million lines of Lean, a language for mathematical proofs. The agents audited the proof and highlighted just one percent of the codebase for human review, a massive time savings. The entire verification process took four weeks, a task that historically takes expert teams years.

The DeepMind analysis did not find any new vulnerabilities in the verified portions of the Signal protocol. To confirm the system could distinguish correct code from buggy code, researchers reintroduced two real, previously fixed bugs into an isolated version of Signal's code; in both cases, AlphaProof Code produced a machine-checked proof that the buggy version was insecure. The researchers are open-sourcing the specification and proof they developed to aid other formal verification work. DeepMind conducted the project as a research effort free of charge and has not disclosed whether it plans to launch a commercial formal verification product.

DeepMind researchers emphasized that the result is just one milestone in a larger process. "We are very excited by this result, but there is a long distance to go before we are able to scale this to all the software of the world, and we want to do that," said Swarat Chaudhuri, a DeepMind research scientist. The research was limited in scope—it did not formally verify the entire Signal mobile app—and scaling AI-assisted formal verification to large volumes of code still requires further development. The team noted that earlier work by the Signal Foundation on formal verification of individual code parts contributed to faster analysis, and they thanked Signal's Rolfe Schmidt, Michael Rosenberg, and Ehren Kret for feedback on the methodology.

stories.headline: DeepMind's Gemini Robotics 2.5 hits 96% success rate packing parts on Mercedes-Benz lines
body: Google DeepMind has unveiled Gemini Robotics 2.5, its latest vision-language-action (VLA) model for robots, reporting a 96% success rate in a real-world pilot on active Mercedes-Benz production lines. The model was tested alongside Apptronik's Apollo 2 humanoid at plants in Kecskemét, Hungary, and Sindelfingen, Germany, where the robots performed automotive kitting — sorting individual parts from bulk bins into sequenced trays for vehicle assembly. According to DeepMind, the pilot shows promising progress toward widespread industrial use, though company director Kanishka Rao cautioned that closing the remaining 4% gap to human-level reliability will be a steep road.

DeepMind says the new model marks a significant advance in dexterity, reliability, and safety. In laboratory evaluations spanning more than 200 tasks — including serving food with tongs, tying a bow on a gift box, and pipetting liquids — Gemini Robotics 2.5 achieved success rates 30% to 100% higher than previous baselines, while completing tasks 20% to 30% faster. Specific improvements over the prior Gemini Robotics 2 model included packing pastries with tongs rising from 5% to 100% success, closing a toolbox lid from 0% to 93%, untying ribbon bows from 0% to 70%, hanging a cardigan from 0% to 62%, and sweeping trash into a dustpan from 0% to 52%. The model works natively with multiple robot platforms, including Apollo 2 with its five-fingered SharpaWave hand (22 degrees of freedom) and the Franka Duo system with two-fingered grippers.

The architecture behind the system combines two components: Gemini Robotics ER, an embodied reasoning model that takes instructions and live video to plan how a robot can accomplish a task, and Gemini Robotics 2.5, the VLA action model that generates the actual movements of actuators, hands, and arms. During the Mercedes-Benz test, the robots picked up metal automotive brackets from supply bins and placed them into sequencing containers, correcting for gaps as they worked. Gemini Robotics ER managed the workflow while Gemini Robotics 2.5 controlled Apollo's hands and arms. Apptronik co-founder and CEO Jeff Cardenas said the pilot is exactly what Apollo was built for — useful work alongside people in real industrial settings — and noted that the models improved dramatically within a few weeks of post-training and carried over to production with very little drop-off.

DeepMind also highlighted safety advances. Gemini Robotics 2.5 uses inference-time reasoning to steer around physical hazards in real time, and company evaluations showed safe task completion increased by 33% around obstacles and 43% near people compared with previous baselines. The company separately introduced ASIMOV-Jailbreak, an open-source benchmark containing hundreds of prompts designed to test whether robotic AI systems resist disguised unsafe instructions. In those tests, the Gemini 4 Argon model achieved a 99.5% resistance rate, compared with 82% for the earlier Gemini Robotics ER 2 model.

Gemini 4 Argon also played a key role in accelerating development of Gemini Robotics 2.5. According to DeepMind, Argon can generate thousands of simulated practice runs from a real-world camera scene, providing varied conditions for training and evaluation. It can also analyze videos of unsuccessful task attempts, suggest possible causes of failure, and help researchers test changes in simulation and on physical robots. Gemini Robotics 2.5 is now rolling out to Google's robotics partners, including Agile Robots, Apptronik, and Boston Dynamics.
